title: La Veta Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: La Veta wells have a 100-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock makes yield and drilling cost vary by lot.
h1: What La Veta Well Records Show Buyers
intro_html:
Buying land near La Veta means evaluating the well record along with the house, access, septic system, and building site. Records for permitted wells within 5 miles show a mountain setting where most wells use unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. Depths and production vary from one lot to the next.

The available records include 473 wells, but only 316 report a total depth and 93 report a pump yield. That makes the local statistics useful for setting expectations, not a guarantee for a particular parcel. A neighboring well search, permit review, and site-specific drilling estimate are important before you commit to land.

sections.heading: La Veta well depth depends on the mountain ground
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near La Veta is 100 feet. The middle half runs from 49 to 236 feet, so a driller bidding a typical job may see something near that range, while still allowing for substantial variation. Half of the recorded wells are under 100 feet, 31% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 14% are between 300 and 600 feet.

The deepest well in the records reaches 2,800 feet. That is not a normal target, but it shows why a simple per-foot estimate cannot remove all risk. Nearly every named aquifer record is an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 464 wells listed that way. Granite and gneiss can change quickly across short distances, making nearby well depth useful context rather than a promise.

sections.heading: What a La Veta well may produce
sections.html:
Among the 93 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces from 5.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute, and 70% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Those figures generally support ordinary household planning when the well, storage, plumbing, and legal water use all fit the property.

Low production is present but not dominant: 2% of reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, while 18% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. A buyer should not treat the 8.0-gpm median as a guaranteed flow rate. Ask for the well construction report, pump test information, storage capacity, and any history of outages. Household-use wells are also subject to Colorado rules, including the exempt-well pumping limit of 35 gallons per minute.

sections.heading: Water levels near La Veta and the measured trend
sections.html:
The recorded median static water level is 35 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 13 to 50 feet. That measurement describes where water stood when the well was checked, not necessarily the amount a pump can deliver during sustained use. Well depth and water level are separate questions when reviewing a property.

The decade series needs careful attention. The median reported water level was 14 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 39 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper measured level in the newer decade, but only 25 records report static water level at all. It suggests a possible local change, not proof of a basin-wide decline. Compare dates, well locations, pumping conditions, and nearby records before drawing a conclusion.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around La Veta, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity is spread across several decades, with the most permits issued in the 2000s at 126. The records show 42 permits in the 1970s, 20 in the 1980s, 73 in the 1990s, 70 in the 2010s, and 36 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. A long permit history gives buyers more neighboring wells to investigate.

Ojo Spring Drilling & Well Service, listed under Blouin, Octave George, appears most often with 98 wells. Timber Line Drilling, listed under Pfaffenhauser, Robert G., appears with 30, and Grande Pump Service & Ojo Sprgs Drlng &, listed under Grande, William M., with 21. These records identify past permit activity, not a guarantee of current availability or a recommendation. Confirm licensing, scope, and references before hiring.

sections.heading: A La Veta drilling budget starts with depth
sections.html:
La Veta’s fractured mountain bedrock is commonly estimated at $65 to $100 per foot for drilling. At the 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone works out to about $6,500 to $10,000. That is a planning range, not a fixed bid, because the final depth, casing, grout, access, and drilling conditions can move the price.

A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,500 to $22,000 at the median depth. Deeper wells can raise the drilling portion substantially, and a difficult mountain-access site may add work outside the basic well price. Get the drilling and completion assumptions in writing, including what happens if the hole is low-yield or dry. Check whether the property already has a permitted well before budgeting for a new one.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building or buying
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk deserve specific questions in La Veta because fractured bedrock is unpredictable. Review nearby permits in La Veta, Walsenburg, Aguilar, Lynn, Gardner, Fort Garland, and Stonewall Gap when they are relevant to the parcel, but give the greatest weight to wells with similar geology and elevation. Confirm the well’s permit status, construction details, pump test, static water level, and actual household performance.

Environmental review also matters. The mapped area includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 63 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. That does not establish contamination at a particular lot. Test existing well water and ask about nearby mines, fill, fuel, and septic systems. For new construction, reserve suitable separation and access for the well, septic system, replacement area, driveway, and utility trenching. Water rights may also require an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a La Veta lot
sections.html:
Start with the parcel’s DWR permit file and the closest neighboring wells. Match reported depths, aquifer descriptions, yields, and water levels to the proposed building area rather than relying on a countywide average. The local record is weighted toward domestic and household use, with 74% listed in that category, while 54% also list stock use. That mix can help explain how nearby wells are being used, but it does not settle your own legal water-use question.

Before closing, have a qualified well professional review the well construction report and pump setup, and obtain a water test from an existing well. If you plan to drill, price access, casing, grout, pump equipment, storage, electrical, trenching, and septic work together. A site that works for a well may not work for a septic system or house foundation. Build the decision around documented water, legal use, and a realistic mountain excavation plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in La Veta?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near La Veta is 100 feet, and the middle half runs from 49 to 236 feet. Half of the records are under 100 feet, but the deepest recorded well reaches 2,800 feet. Because most wells use fractured-bedrock aquifers, nearby records help with planning but cannot guarantee the depth on a specific lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in La Veta?
faq.a: The local drilling estimate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $6,500 to $10,000. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $12,500 to $22,000. Greater depth, difficult access, casing, grout, and site conditions can change the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in La Veta?
faq.a: Among 93 local wells reporting yield, the median is 8.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.0 to 12.0 gallons per minute. About 2% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 18% report from 1 to 5 gallons per minute. Ask for pump-test and storage information instead of relying only on the median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in La Veta?
faq.a: Well water should be tested rather than assumed safe. The mapped area includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 63 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Those locations do not prove a specific well is contaminated. Test an existing well, review its history, and retest after changes to the well, plumbing, or nearby land use.

faq.q: Are La Veta well water levels getting lower?
faq.a: Reported static water levels had a median of 14 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 39 feet in the 2020s, which is deeper in the newer decade. However, only 25 wells report static water level, so the series is limited. Compare measurement dates, pumping conditions, locations, and neighboring wells before treating it as a confirmed area-wide decline.
